chunks: And from him, from Muhammad ibn Abdillah, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from Muawiya ibn Ayyar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I said to him: 'A man makes jewelry for his family worth one hundred dinars, or two hundred dinars, and I think I said three hundred dinars; is Zakat due on it?' He said: 'There is no Zakat on it.' I said: 'Because he fled from Zakat with it?' He said: 'If he fled from Zakat with it, then Zakat is due on it; and if he did it merely to adorn himself with it, then there is no Zakat on it.'
And what Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated is from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Harun ibn Kharij, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I said to him: 'My brother Yusuf was appointed to manage these affairs and acquired much wealth, and he made that wealth into jewelry, intending to flee from Zakat with it; is Zakat due on it?' He said: 'There is no Zakat on jewelry, and what he has brought upon himself of loss by placing it and withholding his own surplus from it is greater than what he fears from Zakat.'

So it is not contradictory to what we mentioned, because the jewelry upon which Zakat is due as a penalty is that which he makes into jewelry after the time of Zakat has arrived; and that upon which Zakat is not due is that which he makes into jewelry at the beginning of the year or before Zakat becomes due on it, and the state continues with it. And what the Imam (peace be upon him) said by 'what he brought upon himself of loss is greater than what he fears from Zakat' refers to what he misses of the reward that if he had left the wealth until the time of Zakat as it was, and did not intend thereby to flee from it, he would have been entitled to it by paying the Zakat from it. And that which indicates this meaning is what was narrated:

key_terms.فَرَّ بِهِ مِنَ الزَّكَاةِ: Fled from Zakat (intention to avoid payment)

ai.seo_question: Is Zakat due on gold jewelry owned by men in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: In *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Shaykh al-Tusi records this ruling from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) distinguishing between jewelry acquired as a strategic asset to avoid Zakat liability versus that acquired for personal adornment. The Imam emphasizes that the primary penalty for 'fleeing' Zakat is not merely the payment itself, but the forfeiture of the spiritual reward and potential growth of the wealth had it remained in its original form until the Zakat due date. This highlights the Shia jurisprudential focus on the intention (*niyyah*) and the opportunity cost of wealth preservation versus spiritual obligation.
